lesson.title: Problem Solving: Putting the Whole Toolkit to Work
lesson.summary: Synthesizes decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design, and stepwise refinement into a single structured problem solving process, applied to a duplicate detection example.
lesson.body:
Every strategy covered so far, decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms, and stepwise refinement, exists to serve one larger goal: solving problems reliably, even ones you have never seen before. Problem solving in computer science is not a single technique, it is the disciplined combination of all the others, applied in a sensible order. A useful general process looks like this: understand what the problem is actually asking, decompose it into smaller pieces, recognize patterns that connect it to problems you already know how to solve, refine a rough plan into precise steps, and only then write and test the code.

Consider the problem: given a list of numbers, determine whether it contains any duplicate values. Understanding the problem means being precise about what counts as a duplicate, in this case, two entries with the same value anywhere in the list, not just next to each other. Decomposition breaks this into a smaller repeated question: "have I already seen this value?" asked once for every element in the list. Pattern recognition notices that "keep track of what I've seen so far while scanning a list" is the same underlying shape as the linear search and all positive examples from earlier sections, just adapted to a new purpose.

A rough plan follows: scan through the numbers, remembering which ones have appeared already, and if any number appears a second time, report that a duplicate was found. Stepwise refinement sharpens "remembering which ones have appeared" into a concrete Python tool, a set, which can check membership quickly and only stores unique values. The refined plan becomes: keep an empty set called seen, for each number check whether it is already in seen, if it is a duplicate exists, if not add it to seen and keep going.

That refined plan translates directly into an algorithm:

def has_duplicates(numbers):
    seen = set()
    for n in numbers:
        if n in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(n)
    return False

Trace this with [4, 2, 7, 2, 9]. seen starts empty. 4 is not in seen, so it gets added: seen is {4}. 2 is not in seen, added: {4, 2}. 7 is not in seen, added: {4, 2, 7}. Now the second 2 arrives: it is already in seen, so the function immediately returns True, correctly detecting the duplicate without needing to check the remaining 9.

This walkthrough shows why problem solving is treated as its own concept, distinct from any single strategy. Abstraction let the solution be wrapped in a clean function with a simple interface. Decomposition and pattern recognition shaped what that function should do internally. Stepwise refinement bridged the gap between a vague idea and working syntax. None of these steps, used alone, would have produced a working, efficient answer nearly as directly as using all of them together, in order, which is the real skill this entire unit has been building toward.
